topics.title: Matter and its properties
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
topics.concept: Matter has mass and occupies space; it exists as solid, liquid or gas, which interconvert. Properties are physical or chemical, extensive or intensive; mixtures are separated by physical methods.

subtopics.title: States of matter and changes of state
subtopics.concept: Solids have fixed shape and volume, liquids fixed volume, gases take the shape and volume of the container. Melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation (solid→gas: iodine, dry ice) and deposition interconvert them. Light, heat and sound are energy, not matter.

subtopics.title: Physical/chemical and extensive/intensive properties
subtopics.concept: Extensive properties depend on the amount of matter (mass, volume, length); intensive properties do not (melting point, boiling point, density, solubility, colour). Magnetic attraction and solubility are physical properties.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

subtopics.title: Separating mixtures
subtopics.concept: Evaporation (crystallisation) recovers a dissolved solid – e.g. salt from sea water in the salt pans of Massawa and Assab; filtration, distillation, sublimation and magnetic separation are other methods.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

topics.title: Atomic structure and formulas
topics.concept: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons; isotopes differ in neutron number; formulas show the number of atoms of each element and give molecular and percentage composition.

subtopics.title: Protons, neutrons, isotopes and average atomic mass
subtopics.concept: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Average atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × fractional abundance).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
textbook_refs.section: 2.2 Subatomic particles – mass number and atomic number

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

subtopics.title: Electron configuration and ion formation
subtopics.concept: Electrons fill shells 2, 8, 8/18 … (transition elements put the 19th+ electrons into the third shell after 4s: Sc = 2, 8, 9, 2). Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration: P (2, 8, 5) → P³⁻.

textbook_refs.section: 1.2 Modern periodic table – electron configuration and transition elements

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

subtopics.title: Chemical formulas, names and empirical formulas
subtopics.concept: Subscripts give the number of atoms; brackets multiply everything inside. Oxyanions: PO₄³⁻ phosphate, PO₃³⁻ phosphite. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio (C₂H₄ → CH₂, H₂O₂ → HO).

Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Molecular mass and percentage composition
subtopics.concept: Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses. % element = (mass of element in formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

subtopics.title: Types of chemical reactions
subtopics.concept: Combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and combustion (a substance burns in oxygen; a hydrocarbon gives CO₂ and H₂O).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.concept: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number. Atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity change periodically.

subtopics.title: Mendeleev's table and the modern periodic table
subtopics.concept: Mendeleev's periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic mass. Defects: position of hydrogen, isotopes (no place for them) and disorder in atomic mass for some pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I). Groups = vertical columns, periods = horizontal rows.

subtopics.title: Periodic trends
subtopics.concept: Across a period the number of shells is constant while the number of valence electrons, ionisation energy and electronegativity increase and atomic radius decreases. Down a group radius increases and electronegativity decreases (K is less electronegative than Li). Isoelectronic ions: the more protons, the smaller the ion.

textbook_refs.section: 1.2 The modern periodic table – groups and periods

subtopics.title: Transition elements
subtopics.concept: d-block elements from Z = 21 (Sc) to 30 (Zn) in period 4, where the inner third shell is being filled.

textbook_refs.section: 1.2 Modern periodic table – electron configuration and transition elements

topics.title: Chemical bonding and intermolecular forces
topics.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
topics.concept: Intramolecular forces (ionic, covalent, metallic bonds) hold atoms together; intermolecular forces (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds) hold molecules together.

subtopics.title: Ionic and covalent bonds; conductivity
subtopics.concept: A single bond shares 2 electrons, a double bond 4, a triple bond 6. Ionic compounds (MgO, NaCl) conduct electricity when molten or dissolved; covalent molecular compounds (CCl₄, CH₄) do not.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
textbook_refs.section: 2.2.1 Ionic bonding – properties of ionic compounds

subtopics.title: Forces of attraction and van der Waals forces
subtopics.concept: Intramolecular forces hold atoms together in a molecule; intermolecular forces hold molecules together. Van der Waals forces: dipole–dipole (polar–polar), dipole–induced dipole (polar–nonpolar, e.g. HCl–H₂) and London/dispersion forces (nonpolar–nonpolar).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

topics.title: Solutions
topics.concept: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures of variable composition. Concentration (molarity = mol/L) measures how much solute is in a given volume; solubility depends on temperature (and pressure for gases); solutes change colligative properties.

subtopics.title: Properties and types of solutions
subtopics.concept: Solutions are clear, homogeneous, cannot be separated by filtration and have variable composition; their properties (boiling/freezing point, vapour pressure) differ from those of the pure solvent. Dilute = little solute relative to solvent; concentrated = much solute.

textbook_refs.section: 3.2 Types of solutions – dilute and concentrated

subtopics.title: Concentration and molarity
subtopics.concept: Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution. Concentration compares particles per unit volume, so halving the volume with half the particles leaves the concentration unchanged.

subtopics.title: Solubility and solubility rules
subtopics.concept: The solubility of a solid changes with temperature; pressure affects only gases (Henry's law). All nitrates and sodium salts are soluble; chlorides are soluble except AgCl, PbCl₂, Hg₂Cl₂; CaSO₄ is only slightly soluble.

subtopics.title: Colligative properties
subtopics.concept: A dissolved solute lowers vapour pressure, raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point. Salt on icy roads works by freezing-point depression.

topics.title: Acids, bases and salts
topics.concept: Acids taste sour and turn litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel slippery and turn litmus blue. pH = −log[H⁺]. Neutralisation and titration use MaVa/na = MbVb/nb.

subtopics.title: Properties and classification of acids and bases
subtopics.concept: Acetic acid CH₃COOH is monoprotic (only the H of –COOH ionises). Bases: bitter, slippery, turn litmus blue, neutralise acids. A bee sting is acidic – treat with a weak base such as calamine lotion; a wasp sting is alkaline – treat with vinegar.

textbook_refs.section: 4.1 Classification of acids – monoprotic and polyprotic

subtopics.title: pH, indicators and titration
subtopics.concept: pH = −log[H⁺]; pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic. Milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) is basic. Common titration indicators: methyl orange, litmus, phenolphthalein. For H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH: mol NaOH = 2 × mol H₂SO₄.

topics.title: Energy and chemical reactions
topics.concept: Energy is kinetic (thermal, electrical) or potential (chemical, gravitational). Exothermic reactions release heat (products have less heat content); endothermic reactions absorb heat. Thermochemical equations are balanced equations with states and ΔH.

subtopics.title: Forms of energy
subtopics.concept: Kinetic energy: energy of motion – thermal and electrical energy. Potential energy: energy of position – chemical and gravitational energy.

textbook_refs.section: 5.1 Energy transformation – kinetic and potential energy

subtopics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions; thermochemical equations
subtopics.concept: Exothermic: heat released, ΔH < 0, H(reactants) > H(products) (combustion, respiration, neutralisation). Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH > 0 (photosynthesis). A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with physical states and ΔH – not a skeletal equation.

subtopics.title: Heat of solution, fusion and other heat changes
subtopics.concept: Heat of solution = enthalpy change when 1 mol of substance dissolves in water; heat of fusion = heat needed to melt 1 mol of a solid (ice +6.01 kJ/mol); heat of combustion, neutralisation, formation and vaporisation are defined per mole.

topics.title: Reaction rates and equilibrium
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
topics.concept: Rate = change in concentration per unit time; it depends on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts. Reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium, which shifts according to Le Chatelier's principle.

subtopics.title: Rate of reaction
subtopics.concept: Average rate = Δ[concentration] ÷ Δt (mol/L·s). Rates change as reactants are used up; they depend on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
textbook_refs.section: 1.1 Measuring the rate of reaction – average rate

subtopics.title: Reversible reactions, equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
subtopics.concept: At equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal and concentrations stay constant. For the exothermic Haber process 3H₂ + N₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, low temperature and high pressure favour ammonia.

topics.title: Oxidation–reduction and electrolysis
topics.concept: Oxidation = loss of electrons / increase in oxidation number; the oxidising agent is reduced. Electrolysis uses electricity to drive non-spontaneous reactions (refining copper, extracting reactive metals, chlor-alkali process, electroplating).

subtopics.title: Oxidation numbers, oxidising and reducing agents
subtopics.concept: Oxidation: loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number (addition of oxygen/removal of hydrogen). In Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, Zn is oxidised (reducing agent) and HCl (H⁺) is the oxidising agent. Mn in KMnO₄ is +7.

subtopics.title: Electrolysis and its applications
subtopics.concept: Uses: purification of copper, extraction of Na/K (Downs cell for molten NaCl), preparation of chlorine and NaOH from brine (H₂ at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode, NaOH as by-product), electroplating/protection against rusting.

topics.title: Nonmetals and their compounds
topics.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Carbon (allotropes, oxides), nitrogen (Haber process) and sulphur (Frasch process, allotropes, contact process) and their compounds.

subtopics.title: Carbon allotropes and carbon monoxide
subtopics.concept: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon (burn to CO₂) but differ: diamond is hard, tetrahedral 3-D network, non-conductor; graphite is soft, layered, conducts electricity. CO combines with haemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and stopping oxygen transport.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Sulphur: Frasch process, allotropes, contact process
subtopics.concept: Frasch process: superheated water melts underground sulphur and hot compressed air forces it to the surface. Rhombic and monoclinic sulphur dissolve in carbon disulphide. Contact process: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum); oleum + water → H₂SO₄.

topics.title: Metals and metallurgy
topics.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Metals are ranked in the activity series; metallurgy is the extraction of metals from ores: enrichment (removal of gangue), roasting/calcination, reduction and refining.

subtopics.title: Activity series and reactivity of metals
subtopics.concept: K, Na react vigorously with oxygen and water; metals above hydrogen (Zn, Fe, Mg) displace H₂ from dilute acids; Cu, Hg, Ag, Pt, Au do not. Copper is fairly unreactive, a good conductor, used in wires and coins, and forms brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn); Eritrea has large copper deposits.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Metallurgy: enrichment, roasting, calcination, reduction
subtopics.concept: Metallurgy = extraction of metals from their ores and their purification. Gangue is removed by physical or chemical methods. Roasting: heating a sulphide ore in excess air → oxide + SO₂. Calcination: heating a carbonate ore in limited air → oxide + CO₂.

topics.title: Behaviour of gases
topics.concept: Gas laws (Boyle, Charles, ideal gas equation PV = nRT, M = dRT/P) and the kinetic molecular theory.

subtopics.title: Gas laws and the ideal gas equation
subtopics.concept: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (T, n constant). Charles: V ∝ T (P, n constant). Ideal gas equation PV = nRT, so molar mass M = dRT/P.

textbook_refs.section: 5.2.5 The ideal gas equation – molar mass and density

subtopics.title: Kinetic molecular theory and ideal gases
subtopics.concept: Molecules have negligible volume, no attractive forces, elastic collisions and average kinetic energy proportional to the absolute temperature. An ideal gas obeys the gas laws under all conditions; real gases approach ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure.

textbook_refs.section: 5.3 The kinetic molecular theory of gases

topics.title: Shapes of molecules and crystals
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
topics.concept: VSEPR predicts molecular shapes; solids are crystalline (unit cells of seven crystal systems) or amorphous.

subtopics.title: VSEPR molecular shapes
subtopics.concept: Two bonding pairs and no lone pairs → linear (CO₂, BeH₂, C₂H₂); two bonding pairs and two lone pairs → bent (H₂O, 104.5°).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

subtopics.title: Crystal systems and amorphous solids
subtopics.concept: The textbook's seven unit-cell shapes: simple cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral, monoclinic, triclinic and hexagonal. Amorphous solids (glass, plastic) have irregular particle arrangement, no definite shape and no sharp melting point.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

topics.title: Organic chemistry
topics.concept: Hydrocarbons (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ saturated; alkenes and alkynes unsaturated) and functional groups (alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters) and their reactions.

subtopics.title: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons; addition and elimination
subtopics.concept: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ are saturated; alkenes CₙH₂ₙ and alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ are unsaturated. HBr adds to an alkene by Markovnikov's rule (H goes to the carbon with more H). Alcohols dehydrate to alkenes with concentrated H₂SO₄.

textbook_refs.section: 2.8 Carboxylic acids – esterification and reaction with bases

subtopics.title: Functional groups and their reactions
subtopics.concept: –OH alcohol, –CHO aldehyde, >C=O ketone (3-pentanone = diethyl ketone), –COOH carboxylic acid, –COO– ester. Acid + alcohol → ester + water (esterification); acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).

textbook_refs.section: 2.8 Carboxylic acids – esterification and reaction with bases

topics.title: Nuclear chemistry
topics.concept: Nuclear stability, radioactive decay (α, β, positron), fission and fusion, uses and hazards of radioactivity.

subtopics.title: Nuclear stability and types of decay
subtopics.concept: All nuclei with Z > 83 are radioactive; bismuth-209 (Z = 83) is the heaviest stable nucleus. α-decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2 (the parent is the decaying nuclide); positron emission converts a proton into a neutron (Z − 1, A unchanged).

textbook_refs.section: 3.1.3 Types of radioactive decay – alpha decay
3.1.3 Types of radioactive decay – positron emission

subtopics.title: Fission, fusion, uses and hazards
subtopics.concept: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into smaller, highly radioactive nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy; fusion powers stars. Uses: medical imaging and treatment, food irradiation, crime detection, water disinfection. Disadvantages: harmful radiation, damage to cells, waste disposal, reactor maintenance.
